market_context: European Union; interpretation of the EU producer code printed on shell eggs.
title: EU Egg Codes 0, 1, 2 and 3: What Free-Range, Barn and Cage Really Mean

seo.title: EU Egg Codes 0, 1, 2 and 3 Explained
seo.meta_description: In the EU, the first digit identifies farming method: 0 organic, 1 free range, 2 barn, 3 cages. The remaining code identifies country and producer.
seo.search_intent: Understand the producer code printed on EU eggs and what it does — and does not — tell shoppers.

excerpt: The first number on an EU egg is not a size or freshness grade. It identifies farming method: 0 organic, 1 free range, 2 barn, and 3 cages. It is followed by the Member State code and producer identification.
content_html:
In the European Union, the first digit stamped on a shell egg identifies the hen production system. The official code uses 0 for organic production, 1 for free range, 2 for barn, and 3 for cages. Letters for the Member State and an establishment identifier follow.

This code is a traceability and farming-method tool. It is not a size grade, freshness score, flavor rating, or nutrition score.

0 means organic production

Zero is used for eggs produced under the applicable organic-production rules. Feed, housing, outdoor access, and other management requirements must satisfy the organic framework.

It should not be read as a universal “zero antibiotics ever” claim or a promise of radically different nutrition. The digit identifies a regulated production system.

1 is free range and 2 is barn

Code 1 means free range: hens are managed under the requirements for outdoor access in that system. Code 2 means barn: hens are not housed in cages, but the system is indoors.

That makes barn and free range different terms. Both may allow movement away from cages, but outdoor access is the central distinction a shopper should understand when comparing 1 and 2.

3 identifies cage production

The number 3 identifies the cage system permitted under current rules. It does not say the egg is microbiologically unsafe, nutritionally inferior, or smaller. It tells you how the hens were housed.

Egg safety depends on sanitary controls, handling, storage, and cooking. Size is communicated separately with S, M, L, and XL rather than with the first producer-code digit.

The following letters and numbers identify origin

After the farming-method digit comes the Member State code — ES for Spain, for example — followed by an identification number assigned to the production establishment by the competent authority. That structure supports traceability back to the producer.

The carton carries additional information such as class, size, dates, and farming-method wording. Reading the shell and carton together prevents a shopper from asking the first digit to tell them more than it was designed to say.

The practical rule: use 0/1/2/3 for farming method, the following letters for country and traceability, and the carton for size, dates, and other attributes. Do not turn one digit into an overall quality score.

When reading an egg carton, separate three ideas: production system, size, and quality or freshness. None of those signals should replace the others. A color, code, or letter tells you about one specific characteristic; it does not by itself summarize nutrition, welfare, safety, or cooking performance.

faq.question: What does 0 mean?
faq.answer: Organic production under the applicable EU rules.

faq.question: What is the difference between 1 and 2?
faq.answer: 1 is free range with regulated outdoor access; 2 is barn housing indoors without cages.

faq.question: Does 3 mean nutritionally worse?
faq.answer: No. Code 3 identifies the cage production system, not a nutrition grade.
